doc.title: Shelly Berg interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Heroes: Oscar Peterson and deciding on jazz at seventeen
summary: Peterson was central; a week in Houston with concerts by Horowitz and Peterson convinced him at about seventeen to be a jazz musician, and his father's 78s shaped him.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Who are the jazz musicians that you aspired to, or just thought that these are the guys man.

It’s a long list. At the center of it all for me growing up was Oscar Peterson. That’s why it was so gratifying to do this album with Ray Brown and that big band tribute album, because that was the motivation. And there was a time I was even going back and forth, classical music, jazz music, what do I want to do. And in one kind of astounding week, Vladimir Horowitz came out of one of his retirements and played in Houston where I was living, and Oscar Peterson came through and did a solo recital in the same hall. And I left the Vladimir Horowitz concert so enthused about practicing and so excited. But I left the Oscar Peterson concert saying that’s what I want to be. And I was about 17 at the time. That’s when it really hit home that I’m going to be a jazz musician, and I’ll always love my classical music but this is it. But growing up my dad exposed me to a lot. He had all the original 78s, Savoy and Dial, all the Charlie Parker and Lucky Thompson and all those great — Don Byas and Coleman Hawkins “Body and Soul” he had all that stuff on 78s. And my dad is a trumpet player so he had probably every Miles Davis album. And he was giving me big dosages of Oscar Peterson and Art Tatum. But I think to this day maybe my favorite player in history is Cannonball Adderley.
